SELECT bm25(entries_fts, 2.0, 8.0, 4.0, 1.0, 1.0, 3.0) AS score,
       e.id, e.title, e.type, e.domain, e.subdomain, e.refutes,

       e.difficulty, e.status, e.body_md, e.path

JOIN entries AS e ON e.id = f.id

ORDER BY score ASC, e.id COLLATE BINARY ASC
LIMIT ?

parent_claims.claim: The literal simultaneous pyramid problem is an interval-permutation problem. Put m=ell+1 and a_i=min(r+i-1,n). If pos(i) is one plus the final row size occupied by colour i, then solutions are exactly permutations satisfying a_i-m+1 <= pos(i) <= a_i+1, clipped to [1,n]. Thus the answer is the permanent of this interval matrix.

Let A_{n,ell,r} denote the answer, with 0<=r<=n and m=ell+1. Then A_{n,ell,0}=1; if r>=1 and m<r, then A_{n,ell,r}=0; and if r>=1, m>=r, and n<m, then A_{n,ell,r}=r!(r+1)^(n-r). For n>=m there is an explicit finite-state formula given below.

Assume 1<=r<=m<=n and set q=m-r. Let U={1-r,...,q}, let S be the q-subsets of U, and I={1,...,q}. Define T_{S,S'} as the number of x in S union {q+1} such that S'={y-1: y in (S union {q+1}) minus {x}} is a q-subset of U. For S={s_1<...<s_q}, put w(S)=r! product_{j=1}^q(s_j+r-j+1). Then A_{n,ell,r}=e_I^T T^(n-m) w.

For fixed ell and r with 1<=r<=m=ell+1, the complete ordinary generating function is rational: G_{ell,r}(z)=sum_{n>=r}A_{n,ell,r}z^n = r! sum_{n=r}^{m-1}(r+1)^(n-r)z^n + z^m e_I^T(I-zT)^(-1)w. Consequently A_{n,ell,r} satisfies an explicit constant-coefficient recurrence of order at most binomial(m,r) for n>=m.

The physical simultaneous problem is generally not the naive intersection of the displacement bounds 'ell left' and 'r right.' For example, n=4, ell=1, r=2 has exactly two physical solutions, represented by 1234 and 1243, whereas the naive two-sided displacement class has seven permutations.

Smallest non-degenerate witness: A = {a_0} (|A| = 1), B = {b_0, b_1, b_2} (|B| = 3), E = {(a_0,b_0), (a_0,b_1), (a_0,b_2)} (i.e. the star K_{1,3}), with m = 3.

Claim says #saturating matchings >= m! = 3! = 6; here #saturating matchings = 3 < 6.

Degenerate (but literally admissible) smallest witness: A = empty, B = empty, E = empty, m = 2. Both hypotheses hold vacuously; the only matching saturating A is the empty matching, so the count is 1 < 2! = 2. This is precisely the configuration the flagged critique points at (H_i with an empty girl side admitting only the 1 empty matching).

Further witnesses in the same family: |A| = 1, |B| = 4, K_{1,4}, m = 4 gives 4 < 24; |A| = 1, |B| = 5, K_{1,5}, m = 5 gives 5 < 120. In general K_{|A|,m} with |A| < m gives m(m-1)...(m-|A|+1) < m! saturating matchings.

All 696 counterexamples found in the searched space have |A| < m, i.e. they violate exactly the dropped hypothesis m <= (number of girls).

The flagged claim: **The proof's induction hypothesis (line 0007) — that ANY bipartite graph with bipartition A,B satisfying Hall's condition for A and with deg(v) >= m for all v in A admits m! matchings saturating A — is false as stated, because it drops the problem's hypothesis m <= (number of girls). The proof never uses m <= n anywhere, and the inductive step (line 0012) breaks exactly at |A| = m, where H_i = G - {a, b_i} has an empty girl side and admits only 1 (empty) matching, not m!.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Induction hypothesis: Suppose any bipartite graph $G$ with bipartition $A,B$, satisfying Hall's condition for $A$, and such that $\deg(v)\geq m$ for all $v\in A$ admits $m!$ matchings saturating all of $A$.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: In the marriage problem, if each girl knows at least $m$ boys, then there are at least $m!$ ways to arrange the marriages.
> 
> I'm finding problems concerning Hall's theorem very difficult even when they're not. (See here for example. I'm sure I wouldn't have come up with the solution in a million years even though it's probably one of the simplest solutions to any problem I've ever seen.) This one is probably easy too, but I have no idea how to approach it. Please, if you can, include in your answers some general tips because I'm starting to feel that I'm not able to learn to think about these things properly.
> 
> Suppose we have $n$ girls and $k$ boys satisfying Hall's condition for the existence of a marriage arrangment such that each girls is given a husband. Suppose additionally that each girl knows at least $m$ boys ($m\leq n$). I'm to show that there are at least $m!$ possible wa [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The quoted induction hypothesis, read literally, is the finitely checkable universal statement: for every integer m >= 1 and every finite bipartite graph G = (A u B, E), if (i) |N(S)| >= |S| for all S subseteq A and (ii) deg(v) >= m for all v in A, then the number of matchings of G saturating A is at least m!. A single finite (G, m) violating the conclusion refutes it, so the claim is finitely refutable and witnesses are finite objects.

The script enumerates ALL labelled bipartite graphs on A = {0..a-1}, B = {0..b-1} for every shape with 0 <= a <= 4, 0 <= b <= 6 and a*b <= 16 (every one of the 2^(a*b) edge sets, 112,949 graphs total), checks Hall's condition by brute force over all 2^|A| subsets, counts A-saturating matchings by an exact integer bitmask DP (the permanent restricted to injections), and tests every m in 1..|B|. 120,179 (graph, m) instances satisfied both hypotheses; 696 of them violated the conclusion. Every reported witness is re-verified from scratch by an independent brute-force count over all injections A -> B via itertools.permutations, and by recomputing degrees and |N(S)| directly. All arithmetic is exact Python ints (math.factorial, bit operations); no floating point enters any decision.

The minimal non-degenerate witness is the star K_{1,3} with m = 3: Hall holds, deg = 3 >= m = 3, but only 3 saturating matchings exist versus the asserted 3! = 6. (Under the alternative reading "admits exactly m! matchings" it also fails: 3 != 6.)

Diagnostic / positive control: the same exhaustive sweep with the dropped hypothesis m <= |A| reinstated yields 117,100 qualifying instances and ZERO violations of "#saturating matchings >= m!". So the inequality is restored exactly by the missing hypothesis m <= n (number of girls), and every counterexample found has |A| < m. This confirms the flagged diagnosis: the induction hypothesis as stated is false because it omits m <= n, and the degenerate endpoint |A| = 0 (empty girl side, 1 empty matching, m! > 1 for m >= 2) is itself a witness -- exactly the configuration the inductive step reaches at |A| = m.

Caveat on scope: the search is exhaustive only within the stated bounds; it establishes existence of witnesses (which it found), not any claim about graphs outside those bounds. Graph isomorphism was not quotiented out, so the 696 count is over labelled graphs.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Minimal witness (found as the smallest of 381 counterexamples over all 91 matroids on <= 4 elements): let M be the uniform matroid U_{1,2} on ground set E = {y, x} (script labels: 0 = y, 1 = x), with independent sets I(M) = { {}, {y}, {x} } (i.e. y and x are parallel elements, rank 1). Take the distinguished element to be x, and let M' be the reduction of M at x used by item (1), namely the contraction M' = M/x, with ground set E - {x} = {y} and I(M/x) = { S subseteq {y} : S + {x} in I(M) } = { {} }, since {x,y} is dependent in M. Now take the solution (independent set) A = {y} in M; note x is NOT in A, so A is not covered by the corrected item (1). Then A' = A - {x} = {y}, and {y} is NOT independent in M' (y is a loop of M/x; rank(M') = 0 < 1 = |A'|), contradicting the sentence "Given any solution A in M, let A' = A - {x}, which is a solution in M' according to (the corrected version of) item (1)." Weighted instantiation with exact integer weights w(x) = w(y) = 1: w(A) = 1, and the proof's intended chain w(B) = w(x) + w_{M'}(B') >= w(x) + w_{M'}(A') >= w(A) cannot even be started, because w_{M'}(A') is undefined — A' is not a solution in M'. Graphic realization for a graph-style DSL: M is the cycle matroid of the multigraph on two vertices u, v with two parallel edges x and y; contracting edge x turns y into a self-loop, so {y} is independent in M but dependent in M/x. Under the alternative reading M' = G - N[x] for independent vertex sets in a graph, the smallest witness is the single-edge graph G = ({0,1}, {01}) with x = 1 and A = {0}: A is independent in G, but A - {x} = {0} is not even a vertex set of G - N[x] = empty graph.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the second direction the proof asserts that for ANY solution (independent set) A in M, the set A' = A - {x} is a solution in M'. This applies item (1), whose (corrected) precondition requires x in A, to arbitrary A; the assertion is false when x is not in A. The proof explicitly defines "solution" as shorthand for "independent set" (line 0013), so "any solution A in M" includes sets not containing x. Because this step is used to conclude w(B) >= w(A) for all independent A, the argument as written does not establish the stated global conclusion "B is a maximum-weight solution in M".**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Given any solution $A$ in $M$, let $A'=A-\{x\}$, which is a solution in $M'$ according to (the corrected version of) item (1).

Context of the original problem:

> Difficulty in understanding the proof of the lemma : "Matroids exhibit the optimal-substructure property"
> 
> I was going through the text *"Introduction to Algorithms" by Cormen et. al.* where I came across a lemma in which I could not understand a vital step in the proof. Before going into the lemma I give a brief description of the possible prerequisites for the lemma.
> 
> ---
> Let $M=(S,\ell)$ be a weighted matroid where $S$ is the ground set and $\ell$ is the family of subsets of $S$ called the independent subsets of $S$. Let $w:S\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be the corresponding weight function ($w$ is strictly positive). 
> 
> Let us have an algorithm which finds an optimal subset of $M$ using greedy method as:
> 
> >$\text{G}{\scriptstyle{\text{REEDY}}}(M,w):$
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts the universally quantified statement (S): for EVERY independent set A of M, A - {x} is an independent set of M'. Item (1), in its corrected form, only licenses this when x is in A, because the reduced structure M' is the contraction M/x whose independent sets are exactly the sets S with S + {x} independent in M (that one-directional implication, with precondition "x in A", is precisely the defining property of contraction; a deletion M \ x would need no such precondition). Consequently, whenever some element y of E - {x} is parallel to x (or more generally whenever A itself is independent in M but A + {x} is dependent), A - {x} = A is independent in M yet dependent in M/x, and (S) fails. The exhaustive search confirms this is not an isolated pathology: over all 91 matroids on ground sets of size <= 4, the contraction reading yields 381 pairs (M, x, A) violating (S), the smallest being U_{1,2} with A = {y}. As a control, under the deletion reading M' = M \ x the same exhaustive sweep found 0 counterexamples (the statement is then trivially true), which pins the flaw precisely on the contraction step the corrected item (1) governs. The failure is exactly the gap the flagging system describes: since the proof's second direction needs w(B) >= w(A) for ALL independent A, and the passage from A to a solution A' of M' is invalid for the (typically most numerous) sets A with x not in A, the argument as written does not establish "B is a maximum-weight solution in M". (Note this refutes the asserted proof step, not necessarily the final theorem, which can be repaired by treating the case x not in A separately, e.g. by an exchange argument replacing some element of A by x.)

## Remarks

- Provenance: record `SE_cs_128091__a128093`, corpus "Stack Exchange, vetted-answer arm (certified)" of the proof-verification canonical-600 confirmed set (commit e33026ae); full dossier in that repository's `iclr_submission/supplement_dossiers.pdf`.

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Use G = K4 with vertices {u,v,a,w} and fixed edge e=uv. Take the Hamilton path P=(u,v,a,w). The endpoint w has non-path neighbors u and v. Choosing z=v gives z != u, but z is at index i=2, not with 2<i<n-1 (here n=4). Thus the stated case split/index claim is false.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Graph Theory_15, solution 2, reads:

> If a neighbor z ∈{x, y} is not u, then z must be some internal vertex vi of the path P (where 2 < i < n − 1).

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/GraphTheory/GT15.lean`):

**Graph Theory_15 (sol2) — an endpoint neighbor `z ≠ u` need NOT be an internal vertex `v_i` with `2 < i < n-1`**

The candidate solution asserts, in the *rotation case* of a Hamilton-path argument:

> "any endpoint neighbor `z` (`≠ u`) must be an internal vertex `v_i` of the Hamilton
>  path `P` with `2 < i < n-1`."

This is false. The neighbor of an endpoint can sit at position `i = 2` (or `i = n-1`),
which is *internal* but does **not** satisfy the strict band `2 < i < n-1`. In fact for
small `n` that band can be empty: at `n = 4` it reads `2 < i < 3`, which no integer
satisfies, so the claim is vacuously refutable as soon as an endpoint has a non-path
neighbor `≠ u` at all.

**Concrete witness — `K₄` with a fixed edge.**
`G = K₄` on vertices `{u, v, a, w}` (`u = 0`, `v = 1`, `a = 2`, `w = 3`) with the fixed
edge `e = uv`. Take the Hamilton path

```
P = (u, v, a, w),   n = 4,   positions  pos(u)=1, pos(v)=2, pos(a)=3, pos(w)=4.
```

The endpoints of `P` are `u` (position `1`) and `w` (position `4`). In `K₄` the endpoint
`w` is adjacent to `u`, `v`, and `a`. The path edge incident to `w` is `a–w`, so the
**non-path** neighbors of `w` are `u` (position `1`) and `v` (position `2`).

Choose `z = v`. Then:

* `z` is a neighbor of the endpoint `w` in `G` (`K₄` adjacency), and `z ≠ u` — so `z`
  satisfies the hypothesis of the rotation case;

> [...]

Minimal witness (found as the smallest of 381 counterexamples over all 91 matroids on <= 4 elements): let M be the uniform matroid U_{1,2} on ground set E = {y, x} (script labels: 0 = y, 1 = x), with independent sets I(M) = { {}, {y}, {x} } (i.e. y and x are parallel elements, rank 1). Now take the solution (independent set) A = {y} in M; note x is NOT in A, so A is not covered by the corrected item (1). Then A' = A - {x} = {y}, and {y} is NOT independent in M' (y is a loop of M/x; rank(M') = 0 < 1 = |A'|), contradicting the sentence "Given any solution A in M, let A' = A - {x}, which is a solution in M' according to (the corrected version of) item (1)." Weighted instantiation with exact integer weights w(x) = w(y) = 1: w(A) = 1, and the proof's intended chain w(B) = w(x) + w_{M'}(B') >= w(x) + w_{M'}(A') >= w(A) cannot even be started, because w_{M'}(A') is undefined — A' is not a solution in M'. Graphic realization for a graph-style DSL: M is the cycle matroid of the multigraph on two vertices u, v with two parallel edges x and y; contracting edge x turns y into a self-loop, so {y} is independent in M but dependent in M/x. Under the alternative reading M' = G - N[x] for independent vertex sets in a graph, the smallest witness is the single-edge graph G = ({0,1}, {01}) with x = 1 and A = {0}: A is independent in G, but A - {x} = {0} is not even a vertex set of G - N[x] = empty graph.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the second direction the proof asserts that for ANY solution (independent set) A in M, the set A' = A - {x} is a solution in M'. This applies item (1), whose (corrected) precondition requires x in A, to arbitrary A; the assertion is false when x is not in A. The proof explicitly defines "solution" as shorthand for "independent set" (line 0013), so "any solution A in M" includes sets not containing x. Because this step is used to conclude w(B) >= w(A) for all independent A, the argument as written does not establish the stated global conclusion "B is a maximum-weight solution in M".**

> Given any solution $A$ in $M$, let $A'=A-\{x\}$, which is a solution in $M'$ according to (the corrected version of) item (1).

Context of the original problem:

> Difficulty in understanding the proof of the lemma : "Matroids exhibit the optimal-substructure property"
> 
> I was going through the text *"Introduction to Algorithms" by Cormen et. al.* where I came across a lemma in which I could not understand a vital step in the proof. Before going into the lemma I give a brief description of the possible prerequisites for the lemma.
> 
> ---
> Let $M=(S,\ell)$ be a weighted matroid where $S$ is the ground set and $\ell$ is the family of subsets of $S$ called the independent subsets of $S$. Let $w:S\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be the corresponding weight function ($w$ is strictly positive). 
> 
> Let us have an algorithm which finds an optimal subset of $M$ using greedy method as:
> 
> >$\text{G}{\scriptstyle{\text{REEDY}}}(M,w):$
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

The sentence asserts the universally quantified statement (S): for EVERY independent set A of M, A - {x} is an independent set of M'. Item (1), in its corrected form, only licenses this when x is in A, because the reduced structure M' is the contraction M/x whose independent sets are exactly the sets S with S + {x} independent in M (that one-directional implication, with precondition "x in A", is precisely the defining property of contraction; a deletion M \ x would need no such precondition). Consequently, whenever some element y of E - {x} is parallel to x (or more generally whenever A itself is independent in M but A + {x} is dependent), A - {x} = A is independent in M yet dependent in M/x, and (S) fails. The exhaustive search confirms this is not an isolated pathology: over all 91 matroids on ground sets of size <= 4, the contraction reading yields 381 pairs (M, x, A) violating (S), the smallest being U_{1,2} with A = {y}. ## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Smallest non-degenerate witness: A = {a_0} (|A| = 1), B = {b_0, b_1, b_2} (|B| = 3), E = {(a_0,b_0), (a_0,b_1), (a_0,b_2)} (i.e. the star K_{1,3}), with m = 3.

Hypotheses of the quoted induction hypothesis all hold: Hall's condition for A holds (the only nonempty subset S = {a_0} has |N(S)| = 3 >= 1), and deg(a_0) = 3 >= m = 3.

Claim says #saturating matchings >= m! = 3! = 6; here #saturating matchings = 3 < 6.

Both hypotheses hold vacuously; the only matching saturating A is the empty matching, so the count is 1 < 2! = 2. This is precisely the configuration the flagged critique points at (H_i with an empty girl side admitting only the 1 empty matching).

All 696 counterexamples found in the searched space have |A| < m, i.e. they violate exactly the dropped hypothesis m <= (number of girls).

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The proof's induction hypothesis (line 0007) — that ANY bipartite graph with bipartition A,B satisfying Hall's condition for A and with deg(v) >= m for all v in A admits m! matchings saturating A — is false as stated, because it drops the problem's hypothesis m <= (number of girls). The proof never uses m <= n anywhere, and the inductive step (line 0012) breaks exactly at |A| = m, where H_i = G - {a, b_i} has an empty girl side and admits only 1 (empty) matching, not m!.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Induction hypothesis: Suppose any bipartite graph $G$ with bipartition $A,B$, satisfying Hall's condition for $A$, and such that $\deg(v)\geq m$ for all $v\in A$ admits $m!$ matchings saturating all of $A$.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: In the marriage problem, if each girl knows at least $m$ boys, then there are at least $m!$ ways to arrange the marriages.
> 
> I'm finding problems concerning Hall's theorem very difficult even when they're not. (See here for example. I'm sure I wouldn't have come up with the solution in a million years even though it's probably one of the simplest solutions to any problem I've ever seen.) This one is probably easy too, but I have no idea how to approach it. Please, if you can, include in your answers some general tips because I'm starting to feel that I'm not able to learn to think about these things properly.
> 
> Suppose we have $n$ girls and $k$ boys satisfying Hall's condition for the existence of a marriage arrangment such that each girls is given a husband. Suppose additionally that each girl knows at least $m$ boys ($m\leq n$). I'm to show that there are at least $m!$ possible wa [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The quoted induction hypothesis, read literally, is the finitely checkable universal statement: for every integer m >= 1 and every finite bipartite graph G = (A u B, E), if (i) |N(S)| >= |S| for all S subseteq A and (ii) deg(v) >= m for all v in A, then the number of matchings of G saturating A is at least m!. A single finite (G, m) violating the conclusion refutes it, so the claim is finitely refutable and witnesses are finite objects.

The script enumerates ALL labelled bipartite graphs on A = {0..a-1}, B = {0..b-1} for every shape with 0 <= a <= 4, 0 <= b <= 6 and a*b <= 16 (every one of the 2^(a*b) edge sets, 112,949 graphs total), checks Hall's condition by brute force over all 2^|A| subsets, counts A-saturating matchings by an exact integer bitmask DP (the permanent restricted to injections), and tests every m in 1..|B|. 120,179 (graph, m) instances satisfied both hypotheses; 696 of them violated the conclusion. Every reported witness is re-verified from scratch by an independent brute-force count over all injections A -> B via itertools.permutations, and by recomputing degrees and |N(S)| directly. All arithmetic is exact Python ints (math.factorial, bit operations); no floating point enters any decision.

The minimal non-degenerate witness is the star K_{1,3} with m = 3: Hall holds, deg = 3 >= m = 3, but only 3 saturating matchings exist versus the asserted 3! = 6. (Under the alternative reading "admits exactly m! matchings" it also fails: 3 != 6.)

Diagnostic / positive control: the same exhaustive sweep with the dropped hypothesis m <= |A| reinstated yields 117,100 qualifying instances and ZERO violations of "#saturating matchings >= m!". So the inequality is restored exactly by the missing hypothesis m <= n (number of girls), and every counterexample found has |A| < m. This confirms the flagged diagnosis: the induction hypothesis as stated is false because it omits m <= n, and the degenerate endpoint |A| = 0 (empty girl side, 1 empty matching, m! > 1 for m >= 2) is itself a witness -- exactly the configuration the inductive step reaches at |A| = m.

Caveat on scope: the search is exhaustive only within the stated bounds; it establishes existence of witnesses (which it found), not any claim about graphs outside those bounds. Graph isomorphism was not quotiented out, so the 696 count is over labelled graphs.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Minimal witness (found as the smallest of 381 counterexamples over all 91 matroids on <= 4 elements): let M be the uniform matroid U_{1,2} on ground set E = {y, x} (script labels: 0 = y, 1 = x), with independent sets I(M) = { {}, {y}, {x} } (i.e. y and x are parallel elements, rank 1). Take the distinguished element to be x, and let M' be the reduction of M at x used by item (1), namely the contraction M' = M/x, with ground set E - {x} = {y} and I(M/x) = { S subseteq {y} : S + {x} in I(M) } = { {} }, since {x,y} is dependent in M. Now take the solution (independent set) A = {y} in M; note x is NOT in A, so A is not covered by the corrected item (1). Then A' = A - {x} = {y}, and {y} is NOT independent in M' (y is a loop of M/x; rank(M') = 0 < 1 = |A'|), contradicting the sentence "Given any solution A in M, let A' = A - {x}, which is a solution in M' according to (the corrected version of) item (1)." Weighted instantiation with exact integer weights w(x) = w(y) = 1: w(A) = 1, and the proof's intended chain w(B) = w(x) + w_{M'}(B') >= w(x) + w_{M'}(A') >= w(A) cannot even be started, because w_{M'}(A') is undefined — A' is not a solution in M'. Graphic realization for a graph-style DSL: M is the cycle matroid of the multigraph on two vertices u, v with two parallel edges x and y; contracting edge x turns y into a self-loop, so {y} is independent in M but dependent in M/x. Under the alternative reading M' = G - N[x] for independent vertex sets in a graph, the smallest witness is the single-edge graph G = ({0,1}, {01}) with x = 1 and A = {0}: A is independent in G, but A - {x} = {0} is not even a vertex set of G - N[x] = empty graph.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the second direction the proof asserts that for ANY solution (independent set) A in M, the set A' = A - {x} is a solution in M'. This applies item (1), whose (corrected) precondition requires x in A, to arbitrary A; the assertion is false when x is not in A. The proof explicitly defines "solution" as shorthand for "independent set" (line 0013), so "any solution A in M" includes sets not containing x. Because this step is used to conclude w(B) >= w(A) for all independent A, the argument as written does not establish the stated global conclusion "B is a maximum-weight solution in M".**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> Given any solution $A$ in $M$, let $A'=A-\{x\}$, which is a solution in $M'$ according to (the corrected version of) item (1).

Context of the original problem:

> Difficulty in understanding the proof of the lemma : "Matroids exhibit the optimal-substructure property"
> 
> I was going through the text *"Introduction to Algorithms" by Cormen et. al.* where I came across a lemma in which I could not understand a vital step in the proof. Before going into the lemma I give a brief description of the possible prerequisites for the lemma.
> 
> ---
> Let $M=(S,\ell)$ be a weighted matroid where $S$ is the ground set and $\ell$ is the family of subsets of $S$ called the independent subsets of $S$. Let $w:S\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ be the corresponding weight function ($w$ is strictly positive). 
> 
> Let us have an algorithm which finds an optimal subset of $M$ using greedy method as:
> 
> >$\text{G}{\scriptstyle{\text{REEDY}}}(M,w):$
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The sentence asserts the universally quantified statement (S): for EVERY independent set A of M, A - {x} is an independent set of M'. Item (1), in its corrected form, only licenses this when x is in A, because the reduced structure M' is the contraction M/x whose independent sets are exactly the sets S with S + {x} independent in M (that one-directional implication, with precondition "x in A", is precisely the defining property of contraction; a deletion M \ x would need no such precondition). Consequently, whenever some element y of E - {x} is parallel to x (or more generally whenever A itself is independent in M but A + {x} is dependent), A - {x} = A is independent in M yet dependent in M/x, and (S) fails. The exhaustive search confirms this is not an isolated pathology: over all 91 matroids on ground sets of size <= 4, the contraction reading yields 381 pairs (M, x, A) violating (S), the smallest being U_{1,2} with A = {y}. As a control, under the deletion reading M' = M \ x the same exhaustive sweep found 0 counterexamples (the statement is then trivially true), which pins the flaw precisely on the contraction step the corrected item (1) governs. The failure is exactly the gap the flagging system describes: since the proof's second direction needs w(B) >= w(A) for ALL independent A, and the passage from A to a solution A' of M' is invalid for the (typically most numerous) sets A with x not in A, the argument as written does not establish "B is a maximum-weight solution in M". (Note this refutes the asserted proof step, not necessarily the final theorem, which can be repaired by treating the case x not in A separately, e.g. by an exchange argument replacing some element of A by x.)
